title: Learning and the Hedgehog - 2
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton argues that schools and teachers often run on a Hedgehog Concept other than learning, and that this quietly distorts everything they do. He catalogues the substitutes: teaching, curriculum, resources, inspections, homework, display, control for new teachers, and subject identity for secondary specialists. Each is a legitimate factor that affects learning but not evidence that learning is occurring. Examples include his own early mentor judging him on pupil learning rather than classroom performance, and a curriculum director who discovered that most staff had never opened five years of documents. The takeaway is a change of question, from asking what we produce or own to asking what its impact on learning is, and it is simple to state but hard to embed.
points: Teacher appraisal that checks teacher behaviour rather than student learning mistakes looking good for being effective.
Curriculum, resources, homework, display and subject expertise all matter, but as factors that serve learning, not as its substitute.
A leader's output, such as shelves of curriculum documents, can become the goal while nobody asks whether students are learning better.
The fix is to reframe every claim as a question of impact, for example whether the iPads are helping each student learn better.
quotes: In other words, teachers are judged against one of many checklists of teacher behaviour that describe whether they look like good teachers rather than whether their students are learning. This is exactly the opposite of how Fred Tiramani, my very early mentor, looked at me.

What I am saying is that a teacher who, for one reason or another, looks ‘good’ at teaching is not sufficient evidence that student learning is happening. At the time of writing, my favourite soccer team has an immaculately kitted, super-fit centre forward who runs around more than anyone else.

Like teaching, a good curriculum is important. It is a guide to both what children should learn and ways to help them learn but it doesn’t guarantee great learning anymore than a good recipe book guarantees good food.

Some schools (and some teachers) have resources as their Hedgehog Concept. From 2010 onwards, these schools talked about having iPads, as though something special is bound to happen when their students use them.

Teachers who are new to the profession often have control as their hedgehog concept. It's a recurring nightmare for new teachers (this is literally true of my first year in teaching) that children and students just won't do what we ask of them.
His Hedgehog Concept had become curriculum document production. That is what his job description made clear, it’s what he was reviewed against and what everyone expected him to do.

Like all organisations, schools have only so much collective energy available to them. If they choose or we insist that they use it up mostly focusing on technology, homework, resources or many of the the other factors that affect learning it drives energy, time and thought away from the question that really matters: is anyone actually getting better?
